asks.title: The promise in one ordinary day
asks.picture: Written play sketch, not a capture: By the end of the first season, the colony has steady turbine power, a modest fog-water supply and a well-used route winding between tall black vine islands. The fuzz keeps moving; small animals come and go beneath it. Daily work still takes planning.
asks.text: What should that colony be able to do comfortably by now, and what should still make stepping outside a considered choice?
asks.why: F1/F2. Your chosen sentence names abundance and insecure footing; it does not yet set the everyday balance between a viable home and a place you must continually negotiate.
asks.guess: A dependable home and a few familiar routes, with journeys beyond them still demanding attention. I would make earned familiarity the payoff while the wider plain remains dangerous.
asks.tree_change: If familiar routes become dependable, the root needs a routine-work/established-route promise alongside wild travel. If even familiar routes remain precarious, acceptance must show sustainable ongoing upkeep rather than implying permanent safety. If the main reward is roaming rather than settling, reorder the root and flagship around expeditions while retaining built colony features. A correction changes the proposed root; silence approves nothing.
asks.decision: Everyday colony promise and root emphasis, without changing the chosen experience sentence.

asks.title: Choosing to cross the thorns
asks.picture: Evidence, then a written play sketch: A historical test sent a drafted colonist on a roughly 113-cell walk across a real Scrub map and the colonist was downed by scratches and venom. That does not prove an ordinary hauling job chose the same route, and its cause was not traced. Now picture a normal hauling order with a long clear way round an island and a much shorter thorny passage through it.
asks.text: What should make a pawn commit to that dangerous passage rather than the clear way round?
asks.why: F2/F3. Dangerous vines are settled scope. The open issue is whether routine work can commit the colony to that risk without a deliberate choice, rather than how much vine should remain or whether its venom should be weaker.
asks.guess: Routine work takes a usable clear detour; a deliberately ordered expedition can accept the thorn route. I would first compare real hauling and explicit crossing on the same two-route fixture.
asks.tree_change: If routine jobs avoid the risk, add a route-choice requirement with clear-detour, no-detour and explicitly ordered crossing cases. If colonists may choose a risky shortcut, acceptance needs the reason the player can understand and a useful way to control that commitment. If only specially prepared pawns should use it, define the preparation and how jobs recognise it. Every answer retains the built hazards and ruled abundance; none declares the old drafted walk proof of a hauling defect.
asks.decision: Routine job commitment to hazardous vine passage versus deliberate expedition.

asks.title: What the Gale asks of the colony
asks.picture: Written play sketch: Forty colonists have workshops, growlights, outdoor haulers and several turbines. The Gale brings extra output, possible breakdowns, muffled outdoor speech and hearing, concealment changes and greater raid weight among threats. The current surge and breakdown interval are provisional numbers.
asks.text: When the Gale starts, what useful change of plan should a well-run colony make?
asks.why: F2. A list of penalties and bonuses can all function while the player simply ignores the weather. The desired decision sets the useful size of the power windfall and maintenance cost.
asks.guess: Use the extra power for worthwhile work while protecting exposed jobs and keeping repair capacity ready. I would judge it by a credible colony plan, without adding an alarm product.
asks.tree_change: A production window needs surplus that materially enables named work and a measurable repair burden. A shelter-and-defend window needs consequences that reward pausing or rerouting outdoor jobs. A mostly ecological spectacle adds no compulsory colony-response leaf; the existing mechanics still receive ordinary checks. His picture tunes consequences; it does not reopen whether those built effects exist.
asks.decision: Meaningful Gale opportunity/cost and tuning target.

asks.title: A day's hunting at the crossing
asks.picture: Written play sketch: The reliable protein is already supposed to be at exposed crossings between covered runways. A hunter watches one: prey under fuzz is visible as a shimmer but cannot be targeted; prey on bare ground can be. Movement in a Stall or a windbreak's calm lee can also expose covered prey. In one version, a skilled hunter spends most of the day there with no useful opening. In another, reading the wind and movement brings a modest but dependable catch. Neither picture is an observed test.
asks.text: What would a good day's hunting at that crossing look like, and what would make you say the promised reliable protein has failed?
asks.why: F2/F3. Reliable interface hunting is already in the biome sheet. Direct invisibility checks do not establish whether ordinary animal movement produces usable hunting opportunities, or whether the player's time and risk pay off.
asks.guess: A competent hunter who chooses the crossing and approach well can usually bring back useful food, with misses and danger still possible. I would test naturally occurring exposure before inventing a new flushing action.
asks.tree_change: If waiting at a well-chosen crossing should pay, require natural exposure and completed hunts over a bounded representative workday. If the hunter must arrange movement or stalk between crossings, define that action and prove it yields a usable shot without removing concealment. If reliability is a season-level supply rather than every workday, use that horizon and include unsuccessful days. This clarifies the settled promise's success bar; it does not reopen protein, crossings or ripple.
asks.decision: Practical time/risk/reward bar for the settled interface-hunting promise.

asks.title: When the premium fuel becomes practical
asks.picture: Written pacing comparison, not measured gameplay: A blanket costs 40 fuzz fiber and 15 sweetline felt, banks one stand for about 30 days at current defaults, then leaves dead cane. Picture A: a small colony sets aside a few stands and uses their premium fuel next season. Picture B: a settled colony tends inherited claims over several seasons before it can rely on the reserve. Both preserve the promised long-and-hot fuel and the trade craft.
asks.text: At what point in a colony's life should that first useful reserve pay back the felt and the wait?
asks.why: F2. Premium fuel is already the purpose; clearing or trade income cannot substitute for it. The unresolved bar is when this seasonal investment should become practical, while scarce felt also has comfortable uses.
asks.guess: A modest reserve should pay off for an established small colony by a later season, with a larger industry taking longer. I would stage the current 30-day cycle and compare its useful burn time with ordinary wood before proposing different numbers.
asks.tree_change: If the next-season small reserve is right, acceptance must show a modest colony can obtain the inputs, tend claims and recover a useful premium reserve in that horizon. If it is a mature multi-season industry, require a sustainable pipeline and an honest long wait, without promising early independence. If it is earlier or later still, his concrete horizon sets timer/yield tuning and the scene duration. Every answer retains the premium fuel advantage, the blanket trade/craft and their separate checks; useful heat superiority must be proved rather than inferred from a fuel filter.
asks.decision: Practical colony stage and time-to-payoff for the settled premium-fuel promise.

asks.title: How the giants find the arsonist
asks.picture: Written play sketch: A colonist lights a patch and runs behind a separate wall. The biome sheet already says the titans come down on the arsonist. Current stamping code damages burning things but does not record or pursue a departed lighter; the calling-pyre separately brings some giants already raging. Compare a giant that saw the act, one that arrives after the person vanished, and an innocent worker beside the spreading fire.
asks.text: How should the giants connect the fire to its maker, and what could that person do to escape them?
asks.why: F2/F3. The arsonist being at risk is settled. Attribution, pursuit and escape are not specified by that promise, and cannot silently be replaced by ritual-style hostility to everybody.
asks.guess: The giants follow a readable physical connection to the act or its immediate source, with a chance to break contact and escape. I would show the three cases before binding any rule that gives them knowledge across walls.
asks.tree_change: Witnessed action needs attribution when the giant can perceive the act and a defined loss-of-contact rule. A persistent trail needs an actual readable trace, finite pursuit and an escape case. A broader association with nearby fire-making needs a concrete identification rule and an innocent-worker control. Under every answer, the arsonist remains the promised target; ordinary stamping and the ritual's raging arrivals keep separate acceptance.
asks.decision: Believable attribution, pursuit and escape for the settled arsonist consequence.

asks.title: A visit that appears only in the tree's memory
asks.picture: Written play sketch: You watch a sweetline tree throughout the day. Its history then says a road-party camped under it, or a pilgrim left a token, but no person ever appeared. That is how visits are currently implemented: counters, ash or tokens rather than arriving pawns.
asks.text: What must happen in the world for the tree's history to call something a visit?
asks.why: F2/F3. Existing visits are built and historically tested, but a passing counter test cannot decide whether remembered travellers are enough for the living-road promise.
asks.guess: For a visit dated during play, I would expect someone to arrive and stay if the player watches throughout. Timed traces remain a valid existing mechanism; I would first make the claim about them honest before treating a counter as proof of a person.
asks.tree_change: If timed traces are the intended representation, retain the ongoing timer, marks and counters, with wording and acceptance that honestly describe those traces. If a live visit must include people, add arrival, time under the tree, departure and token/history agreement to the existing timed system, reusing suitable visitor/camp services. A different explanation must still account for the ongoing visit event. No answer removes the built timer or restores bark-wardens or farmer factions.
asks.decision: Truth of live tree visits versus abstract history.

root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: LeaningScrub is an endless moving fuzz plain where steady wind makes power plentiful and tall, dangerous venomvine makes footing costly. One wind shapes the plants, carries scent and drives fire, through a rich soundscape of small life. Beneath the canopy, a passing body sets off a wave of scattering, swaying and surfacing creatures; some burst into the air, others shed a twitching arm or retreat toward their home. The Stall exposes movement, while the Gale brings noise, turbine surges and breakdown risk, and a busier plain. Venomvine forms make islands with different dangers and rewards, creeping slowly downwind while the colony works its ways through. Fuzz and sweetline felt become blankets that bank premium fuel for future seasons; rare named sweetline trees gather coats, shed felt and keep a history. Dead farmsteads teach powered fog-water harvesting, and eligible scavenger clans can inhabit the land. Open fires bring giants down on the blaze and its maker; the calling-pyre makes that danger a deliberate, costly act. A viable home is possible here, but its people must earn their routes, read the wind and respect the life concealed beneath their feet.

neighbours.text: Base thicket, body-size barriers, contact venom, trap/race immunity and global hazard settings. LeaningScrub opts in through comps and registered mechanic gates; special lash routes must respect the promised settings boundary.
Surrik swim/strike, home tether/scoped aggression and shared SunGeometry. Reuse and verify those opt-ins rather than building rival AI.
Packaging and shell; sweetline canopy renderer extension lives in shared Biomes code. Own folder presence is not deployed package truth.
Franchise roster, thunderstep stamper and existing scavenger-clan choices. Own-RM fauna appearance bars are distinct from this cast. No new faction invented.

Giant physical passage/warnings are a separate service. LeaningScrub fire-stamp marker/kind choice is not automatically a native T2+ passage roster. LEANINGSCRUB_TITAN_POPULATE_SCRUB_UNSTOMPED remains a roster/passers task, not a new generic engine.
Venomvine explicitly opts out of soak and ordinary growth bands. Sweetline longevity is separately ruled; no dry-scar system inferred.
Existing optional payload, guarded and string-resolved. Not authority to construct the prohibited ecology-warning product.

CompSpawner water production, techprints/research, food-search scavenging, shearing coats, ritual framework and fuel filters already do those jobs. Acceptance must use them, rather than infer play from static hook checks.
